- Any $2\times 3$ matrix $A$ has at most $2$ distinct singular values.
- The matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]$ has one negative singular value.
- Any $5\times 3$ matrix $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values." :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since $A$ is a $2\times 3$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $3\times 3$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{3\times 2}\times {A}_{2\times 3}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{3\times 3}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is false. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, $A$ can't have a negative singular value.

- Statement III is true. Since $A$ is a $5\times 3$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $3\times 5$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $3\times 3$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{3\times 5}\times {A}_{5\times 3}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{3\times 3}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-389a199b-2132-5200-92d1-2261a44348a8"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-389a199b-2132-5200-92d1-2261a44348a8" :answer-field/id #uuid "389a199b-2132-5200-92d1-2261a44348a8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-5ec6c063-a755-58f5-8636-29649c9e3395" :answer-field/choices ["answer-7c2cf85b-73a0-5874-97a9-cfa33e64d6b5" "answer-e71d59cc-b53d-52ee-9d28-5a2450433b8d" "answer-4c278b14-28c2-57de-b60a-2a720876d406" "answer-5b060c6a-de3b-54b0-bfda-579bbdcbb6d0" "answer-5ec6c063-a755-58f5-8636-29649c9e3395"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7c2cf85b-73a0-5874-97a9-cfa33e64d6b5" :answer/id #uuid "7c2cf85b-73a0-5874-97a9-cfa33e64d6b5" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e71d59cc-b53d-52ee-9d28-5a2450433b8d" :answer/id #uuid "e71d59cc-b53d-52ee-9d28-5a2450433b8d" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4c278b14-28c2-57de-b60a-2a720876d406" :answer/id #uuid "4c278b14-28c2-57de-b60a-2a720876d406" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5b060c6a-de3b-54b0-bfda-579bbdcbb6d0" :answer/id #uuid "5b060c6a-de3b-54b0-bfda-579bbdcbb6d0" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5ec6c063-a755-58f5-8636-29649c9e3395" :answer/id #uuid "5ec6c063-a755-58f5-8636-29649c9e3395" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186184880 :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true?

- Any $6\times 8$ matrix $A$ has at most $8$ distinct singular values
- Any $10\times 8$ matrix $A$ has at most $10$ distinct singular values.
- The matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]$ has two non-negative singular values." :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, since $A$ is a $6\times 8$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $8\times 6$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $8\times 8$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{8\times 6}\times {A}_{6\times 8}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{8\times 8}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $8$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is false. Since $A$ is a $10\times 8$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $8\times 10$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $8\times 8$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{8\times 10}\times {A}_{10\times 8}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{8\times 8}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $8$ distinct singular values.

- Statement III is true.  Indeed, all singular values of any matrix are non-negative.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-2360b526-d791-5f7a-b1d6-add9140e9172"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-2360b526-d791-5f7a-b1d6-add9140e9172" :answer-field/id #uuid "2360b526-d791-5f7a-b1d6-add9140e9172" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-7ad14134-11d1-5b66-b73a-b208f1547b8a" :answer-field/choices ["answer-058c04c6-70ed-5f40-82ed-2d503073a803" "answer-7ad14134-11d1-5b66-b73a-b208f1547b8a" "answer-ef49fb2b-88b6-550b-873b-58a76d4cd449" "answer-21ea85fd-6292-5db7-9dc1-8fed164bc983" "answer-dc81e283-4f32-52f2-9dc0-2d02dfad8da9"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-058c04c6-70ed-5f40-82ed-2d503073a803" :answer/id #uuid "058c04c6-70ed-5f40-82ed-2d503073a803" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7ad14134-11d1-5b66-b73a-b208f1547b8a" :answer/id #uuid "7ad14134-11d1-5b66-b73a-b208f1547b8a" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ef49fb2b-88b6-550b-873b-58a76d4cd449" :answer/id #uuid "ef49fb2b-88b6-550b-873b-58a76d4cd449" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-21ea85fd-6292-5db7-9dc1-8fed164bc983" :answer/id #uuid "21ea85fd-6292-5db7-9dc1-8fed164bc983" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-dc81e283-4f32-52f2-9dc0-2d02dfad8da9" :answer/id #uuid "dc81e283-4f32-52f2-9dc0-2d02dfad8da9" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-e69dd032-aa5c-5891-a7fc-97b84703e88a" :question/id #uuid "e69dd032-aa5c-5891-a7fc-97b84703e88a" :question/math-academy-id "q-95261" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true?

Hence, $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f8cda2f1-5552-5357-82cc-f1ab61cac36e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-f8cda2f1-5552-5357-82cc-f1ab61cac36e" :answer-field/id #uuid "f8cda2f1-5552-5357-82cc-f1ab61cac36e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-4d306b2f-e020-5c0b-8b36-318a141afa1a" :answer-field/choices ["answer-4d306b2f-e020-5c0b-8b36-318a141afa1a" "answer-d11ab6aa-4e8f-5b94-8bb5-66fd5a8105bf" "answer-884aa6f5-9cee-5d6c-a6d2-1e3e9fda993d" "answer-f351ce40-cb01-5b7d-a5fb-a7f513b6a235" "answer-c41c10ba-d192-5a1a-9031-b8c0dab1e30f"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4d306b2f-e020-5c0b-8b36-318a141afa1a" :answer/id #uuid "4d306b2f-e020-5c0b-8b36-318a141afa1a" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d11ab6aa-4e8f-5b94-8bb5-66fd5a8105bf" :answer/id #uuid "d11ab6aa-4e8f-5b94-8bb5-66fd5a8105bf" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-884aa6f5-9cee-5d6c-a6d2-1e3e9fda993d" :answer/id #uuid "884aa6f5-9cee-5d6c-a6d2-1e3e9fda993d" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f351ce40-cb01-5b7d-a5fb-a7f513b6a235" :answer/id #uuid "f351ce40-cb01-5b7d-a5fb-a7f513b6a235" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c41c10ba-d192-5a1a-9031-b8c0dab1e30f" :answer/id #uuid "c41c10ba-d192-5a1a-9031-b8c0dab1e30f" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-fef86daf-091a-52fa-bcf0-1d2b609bb348" :question/id #uuid "fef86daf-091a-52fa-bcf0-1d2b609bb348" :question/math-academy-id "q-95281" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true?

:question/problem "What are the singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}]?$" :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ -1 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}17 & -8 \\ -8 & 17\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}17-\lambda  & -8 \\ -8 & 17-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (17-\lambda )(17-\lambda )-64 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-34\lambda +289-64 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-34\lambda +225 & =0 \\ (\lambda -9)(\lambda -25) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =25,\,9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{25}=5 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{9}=3\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-186b2a25-d332-5f01-a6a2-293d5802ee3e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id the singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]?$" :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 0 \\ 0 & 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}9-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 9-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (9-\lambda )(9-\lambda ) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{9}=3\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-533bf985-e003-5103-b11c-9c7a7c723cb4"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-533bf985-e003-5103-b11c-9c7a7c723cb4" :answer-field/id #uuid "533bf985-e003-5103-b11c-9c7a7c723cb4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-3c2115b7-3deb-582b-a761-e79b45a72ba3" :answer-field/choices ["answer-872eaed5-b7dd-5088-8dd0-359491c4f657" "answer-3c2115b7-3deb-582b-a761-e79b45a72ba3" "answer-72a19815-f7b7-56e9-badf-ea7b9e73091b" "answer-949e815d-00ae-5171-94b0-1798b1a30df1" "answer-93dcd708-1476-51b0-ac1f-9db7ca101165"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-872eaed5-b7dd-5088-8dd0-359491c4f657" :answer/id #uuid "872eaed5-b7dd-5088-8dd0-359491c4f657" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$3,$ $1$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3c2115b7-3deb-582b-a761-e79b45a72ba3" :answer/id #uuid "3c2115b7-3deb-582b-a761-e79b45a72ba3" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$3,$ $3$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-72a19815-f7b7-56e9-badf-ea7b9e73091b" :answer/id #uuid "72a19815-f7b7-56e9-badf-ea7b9e73091b" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$6,$ $1$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-949e815d-00ae-5171-94b0-1798b1a30df1" :answer/id #uuid "949e815d-00ae-5171-94b0-1798b1a30df1" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$9,$ $3$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-93dcd708-1476-51b0-ac1f-9db7ca101165" :answer/id #uuid "93dcd708-1476-51b0-ac1f-9db7ca101165" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$9,$ $6$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186185322 :tutorial/content "Recall that the singular values of a real matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$

Also, since $A^T \! A$ is a positive semi-definite matrix, the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A$ must be always non-negative real numbers.

Let's compute the singular values of the matrix $A,$ given by 

![](images/a9/a9edbe1fee59758c9557d95ea8f62468f9f3cb98449c437a274bdbf5c30f7dc6.svg)

Now, since

- $A$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix, and

- $A^T$ is a $2 \times 3$ matrix,

then $A^T \! A$  must be a $2 \times 2$ matrix:

$$
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times {\large 3}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 3} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A} = 
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A^T \! A}
$$

Let's now compute our singular values. First, we calculate $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 2 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}8-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (8-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda +36 & =0 \\ (\lambda -9)(\lambda -4) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- When listing the singular values of a matrix, we usually write them in descending order.

- If $A$ is a $m\times n$ matrix, then $A^T A$ is a $n\times n$ positive semi-definite matrix. This means that $A$ has *at most* $n$ distinct singular values." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186184404 :activity/expected-seconds 660.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

$$

- Statement II is false. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, $A$ can't have a negative singular value.

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{3\times 5}\times {A}_{5\times 3}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{3\times 3}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

A.$

Also, since $A^T \! A$ is a positive semi-definite matrix, the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A$ must be always non-negative real numbers.

Let's compute the singular values of the matrix $A,$ given by 

![](images/a9/a9edbe1fee59758c9557d95ea8f62468f9f3cb98449c437a274bdbf5c30f7dc6.svg)

Now, since

- $A$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix, and

- $A^T$ is a $2 \times 3$ matrix,

then $A^T \! A$  must be a $2 \times 2$ matrix:

$$
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times {\large 3}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 3} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A} = 
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A^T \! A}
$$

Let's now compute our singular values. First, we calculate $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 2 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}8-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (8-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda +36 & =0 \\ (\lambda -9)(\lambda -4) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- When listing the singular values of a matrix, we usually write them in descending order.

- If $A$ is a $m\times n$ matrix, then $A^T A$ is a $n\times n$ positive semi-definite matrix. This means that $A$ has *at most* $n$ distinct singular values." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186184404 :activity/expected-seconds 660.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}] "assertions" [[17592186184095 :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true?

["question-e69dd032-aa5c-5891-a7fc-97b84703e88a" :question/math-academy-id "q-95261"] ["question-e69dd032-aa5c-5891-a7fc-97b84703e88a" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true?

- Any $4\times 3$ matrix $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.
- The singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -2 & -3\end{aligned}]$ are non-negative.
- Any $3\times 4$ matrix $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values."] ["question-e69dd032-aa5c-5891-a7fc-97b84703e88a" :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Since $A$ is a $4\times 3$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $3\times 4$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $3\times 3$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{3\times 4}\times {A}_{4\times 3}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{3\times 3}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is true. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative.

- Statement III is false. Since $A$ is a $3\times 4$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $4\times 3$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $4\times 4$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{4\times 3}\times {A}_{3\times 4}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{4\times 4}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only.""] ["question-e69dd032-aa5c-5891-a7fc-97b84703e88a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["question-fef86daf-091a-52fa-bcf0-1d2b609bb348" :question/math-academy-id "q-95281"] ["question-fef86daf-091a-52fa-bcf0-1d2b609bb348" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true?

- The matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]$ has one negative singular value.
- Any $4\times 5$ matrix $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values."] ["question-fef86daf-091a-52fa-bcf0-1d2b609bb348" :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$

- Statement III is false. Since $A$ is a $4\times 5$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $5\times 4$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $5\times 5$ matrix:

$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $5$ distinct singular values.

eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ -1 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}17 & -8 \\ -8 & 17\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}17-\lambda  & -8 \\ -8 & 17-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (17-\lambda )(17-\lambda )-64 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-34\lambda +289-64 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-34\lambda +225 & =0 \\ (\lambda -9)(\lambda -25) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =25,\,9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{25}=5 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{9}=3\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-97ca7c6b-3d02-595e-9b24-0e63b350342b" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-186b2a25-d332-5f01-a6a2-293d5802ee3e" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

"The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 0 \\ 0 & 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}9-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 9-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (9-\lambda )(9-\lambda ) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{9}=3\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-ab4ca253-4533-55ea-9cf5-518c8864d1f6" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-533bf985-e003-5103-b11c-9c7a7c723cb4" :answer-field/id #uuid A.$

Also, since $A^T \! A$ is a positive semi-definite matrix, the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A$ must be always non-negative real numbers.

Let's compute the singular values of the matrix $A,$ given by 

![](images/a9/a9edbe1fee59758c9557d95ea8f62468f9f3cb98449c437a274bdbf5c30f7dc6.svg)

Now, since

- $A$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix, and

- $A^T$ is a $2 \times 3$ matrix,

then $A^T \! A$  must be a $2 \times 2$ matrix:

$$
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times {\large 3}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 3} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A} = 
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A^T \! A}
$$

Let's now compute our singular values. First, we calculate $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 2 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}8-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (8-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda +36 & =0 \\ (\lambda -9)(\lambda -4) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- When listing the singular values of a matrix, we usually write them in descending order.

- If $A$ is a $m\times n$ matrix, then $A^T A$ is a $n\times n$ positive semi-definite matrix. $$

$$

0\end{aligned}]?$" :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & -1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 5 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 5-\lambda  & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & -2 \\ -2 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}|-4|\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ 0 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )[(5-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-4)]-16(4-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-9\lambda +16)-16(4-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-9\lambda ) & =0 \\ \lambda (4-\lambda )(\lambda -9) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,4,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )((1-\lambda )^{2}-1) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(1-2\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}-1) & =0 \\ -\lambda (\lambda -1)(\lambda -2) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =2,\,1,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{2} \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{1}=1 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}

[{:db/id 17592186184968 :step/content {:db/id 17592186185322 :tutorial/content "Recall that the singular values of a real matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$

Also, since $A^T \! A$ is a positive semi-definite matrix, the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A$ must be always non-negative real numbers.

Let's compute the singular values of the matrix $A,$ given by

$$A= [\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].$$

Now, since

- $A$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix, and
- $A^T$ is a $2 \times 3$ matrix,

then $A^T \! A$ must be a $2 \times 2$ matrix:

$$\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times {\large 3}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 3} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A} = \underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A^T \! A}$$

Let's now compute our singular values. First, we calculate $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 2 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}$$

Next, we compute the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}8-\lambda & 2 \\ 2 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (8-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda +36 & =0 \\ (\lambda -9)(\lambda -4) & =0 \\ \lambda & =9,\,4\end{aligned}$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2\end{aligned}$$

Note the following:

- When listing the singular values of a matrix, we usually write them in descending order.
- If $A$ is a $m\times n$ matrix, then $A^T A$ is a $n\times n$ positive semi-definite matrix. This means that $A$ has *at most* $n$ distinct singular values." :tutorial/id #uuid "6230f35e-b526-5e84-be30-86c8cdcbd301" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4891 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}8-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (8-\lambda )(2-\lambda ) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =8,\,2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{8} \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )((1-\lambda )^{2}-1) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(1-2\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}-1) & =0 \\ -\lambda (\lambda -1)(\lambda -2) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =2,\,1,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{2} \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{1}=1 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}

$$

[17592186046660 1008 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences II continues the development of advanced mathematical techniques used throughout modern physics. Building on the analytical framework established in the first course, students study orthogonality, multivariable integration, vector calculus theorems, and advanced methods for differential equations.
The course emphasizes mathematical structures that arise naturally in physics, including inner product spaces, orthogonal projections, integral theorems of vector calculus, and transform methods for solving differential equations. These tools provide the mathematical foundation for analyzing electromagnetic fields, wave phenomena, dynamical systems, and statistical models encountered in advanced physics courses." 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1009 "The course begins with the theory of projections in inner product spaces. Students study norms, inner products, orthogonality, and orthogonal complements in vector spaces over the real and complex numbers. Techniques such as orthogonal projections, the Gram–Schmidt process, and QR factorization allow vectors to be decomposed into orthogonal components. These ideas play a role in Fourier analysis, signal decomposition, and numerical methods used in physical simulations.
Students then explore quadratic forms and the diagonalization of symmetric matrices. The spectral theorem provides a geometric interpretation of symmetric transformations and leads to techniques for analyzing energy functions and stability in physical systems. Singular value decomposition is also introduced as a powerful matrix factorization with applications in numerical modeling and data analysis.
Applications of linear algebra follow, including least-squares methods for solving overdetermined systems. These methods arise when fitting theoretical models to experimental data and when approximating solutions to physical equations.
The course then develops multivariable integration in three dimensions. Students compute triple integrals over general regions and apply coordinate transformations such as cylindrical and spherical coordinates. These techniques allow physicists to compute quantities such as mass distributions, charge densities, and gravitational or electric potentials.
Students next study line integrals and surface integrals of scalar and vector fields. Concepts such as circulation, flux, and path independence lead to the fundamental theorems of vector calculus, including Green’s theorem, the divergence theorem, and Stokes’ theorem. These results form the mathematical framework underlying conservation laws and the differential and integral formulations of electromagnetic theory.
Applications of multivariable calculus follow, including vector mechanics and optimization. Students analyze motion using vector-valued functions, apply Newton’s second law to systems in the plane, and study work–energy relationships. Multiple integrals are used to compute mass, centers of mass, moments of inertia, and other physical quantities.
The course then returns to differential equations, extending earlier techniques to systems of linear differential equations. Students analyze dynamical systems using eigenvalues, phase portraits, and matrix methods, which appear in models of interacting systems such as coupled oscillators or predator–prey dynamics.
Laplace transforms are introduced as a powerful tool for solving linear differential equations with discontinuous inputs or initial conditions. Boundary value problems and Fourier series are then developed, providing mathematical techniques used to solve differential equations describing heat flow, vibrating strings, wave propagation, and other physical phenomena.
The course concludes with numerical methods for differential equations and advanced probability topics. Students analyze the accuracy and stability of numerical schemes used in computational physics and study multivariate probability distributions and the central limit theorem, which appear in
